parts.title: Joining a Car-Share Club
parts.context: A woman phones a city car-share club to become a member.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a car-share club to become a member. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 7.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Harbour Car Share, Craig speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, hi, Craig. I'd like to join the club, please. The online form kept freezing on me, so I thought I'd just ring.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Yeah, sorry about that. No worries, I can do it over the phone. Can I start with your name?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Sure. It's Joanna Pellowe.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: And how do you spell the surname?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: P... E... double L... O... W... E.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: P... E... double L... O... W...

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Sorry, there's an E on the end as well. People always leave it off.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Got it, with the E. And your home address?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: It's flat six, forty-two Lennox Street, in Rozelle.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Lennox Street... and the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Two-oh-three-nine... no, hang on, that's the office. Home is two-oh-three-seven.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Two-oh-three-seven. Lovely. Now, we ask everyone what they'll mainly be using the cars for. Is it mostly for work, or...?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Not for work, no. I cycle to the office. I used to borrow a friend's car to take my sister to the airport, but she's moved to Perth now, so... these days it'd mostly be to drive up and see my grandmother. She lives in a little town in the Blue Mountains, and the train doesn't go all the way.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Yeah, the trains up there aren't great at weekends. And which of our car bays would be handiest for you? In Rozelle we've got three.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Well, the one at the light rail stop would be ideal, but every time I've looked on the map, the cars there are booked out. Craig: That one's very popular, I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And the bay outside the library, I thought that'd be the closest, but...

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Ah, that one's actually closed till the end of the year. The council's digging up the road there.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Right, then put me down for the one behind the swimming pool. It's only a five-minute walk, so that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Behind the pool, no problem. You can change that any time in the app anyway. Now, we've got three plans. There's Casual, which has no monthly fee but higher hourly rates; there's Plus, which has a small monthly fee and cheaper hours; and Premium, which is really for people who drive most days.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I was thinking Casual, because I honestly won't drive that much. Maybe twice a month?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: You could. But two return trips to the mountains a month, they're long bookings, say six or seven hours each. On Casual you'd be paying the higher rate the whole time. I reckon the middle one would work out cheaper for you.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Hmm... yeah, if they're full-day trips... Okay, you've talked me into it. I'll go for Plus. Not Premium, though, that's way more than I need.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Fair enough. Plus it is.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And what's the monthly fee on that? The website said twelve dollars fifty.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Ah, that's last year's figure, the page hasn't been updated. It went up in July. It's fourteen dollars ninety-five a month now.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Fourteen ninety-five. Okay. Still a lot cheaper than running my own car.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Definitely. Now, we'll need a scan of your driver's licence, front and back, and something showing your address. A bank statement's fine...

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I don't get paper statements any more. It's all online, and the screenshots don't actually show my address.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Right. We used to take mobile phone bills, but we can't accept those any more, head office changed the rules. Have you got a gas or an electricity bill?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: The gas is in my flatmate's name, but I can send you my electricity bill, that's got my name and address on it.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Perfect. Just email it to us with the licence scan.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 8 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Can I ask about the rules? What happens if I'm late bringing a car back? The traffic coming down from the mountains can be awful on a Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: It happens. If you can, extend the booking in the app before it runs out. If you don't, there is a charge. It used to be a flat twenty-five dollars, whatever happened, which people thought was a bit harsh if they were only five minutes over.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I can imagine.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: So now it's worked out in blocks of fifteen minutes. You pay a small fee for each block you're over. We don't charge you for a whole extra hour, which is what some of the other clubs do.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: That sounds fairer. And is there anything I have to do before I drive off? Do I need to ring you?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: You don't need to call us. That's what we used to ask, but the app does all that now. Some members check the petrol gauge, but honestly, our staff refuel the cars, and there's a fuel card in the glovebox if you do run low, so that's not something you need to worry about.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, right. Craig: The one thing we do insist on is that you walk around the car and take pictures of any scratches or dents in the app. Otherwise you could end up getting blamed for them.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Good to know. I'll make sure I do that.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: So, would you like to make your first booking now? Your membership card takes about five days to come in the post.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, so I'd have to wait for that anyway?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: No, no, you don't need the card. Once your documents are approved, you can unlock the cars with your phone. That's usually the same day.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, good. I was hoping to go up this Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Let me see... yep, the hatchback behind the pool is free all day Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Actually... I'd better not book it yet. My grandmother sometimes goes to her bridge club on a Saturday, and I don't want to drive all that way if she isn't going to be home. I'll ring her tonight and then book it in the app.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: No problem at all. I'll email you a link to the app in the next few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Great. Thanks so much for your help, Craig.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: My pleasure, Joanna. Enjoy the drive.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: The Ashcombe Heritage Trail
parts.context: A local radio presenter introduces the council's heritage officer, who describes a new heritage trail in the town.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter introducing a heritage officer, who is talking about a new heritage trail in her town. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 16.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Good morning, and welcome back to Ashcombe Today. Now, those small metal discs that have appeared in the town centre pavements are part of the new Ashcombe Heritage Trail, which opens this Saturday, and here to tell us all about it is the council's heritage officer, Ruth Penhale. Morning, Ruth.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Morning, Steve, and thanks for having me. Well, the trail links fourteen places of interest in the old town, but this morning I'll just pick out six of the main ones.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Let's start at the Corn Exchange on the High Street. A lot of people still think of it as the place to get a coffee, and there was a café on the ground floor for years, but it closed last spring and the space is empty for now. What you will find just inside the entrance hall is a model of the town as it looked in about eighteen fifty. It was built by pupils from Ashcombe Primary as a class project last term, and it's remarkably detailed. They even put tiny sheep in the market square.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: From there, the trail goes down Well Lane to St Bride's Well. This is one of the oldest sites in the town; there's been a spring there since medieval times. We'd originally planned to put one of our audio posts there, where you press a button and hear a short recording, but the budget didn't stretch that far, sadly.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: And I should warn listeners: the well sits at the bottom of a flight of very narrow, uneven steps. We did look into putting in a ramp, but because the stonework is protected, we weren't given permission. So I'm afraid it isn't a stop that anyone in a wheelchair will be able to get down to.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Just past the well, you come to the Tannery Bridge over the river. Now, generations of Ashcombe people have called it the black bridge, because that's the colour it's been for as long as anyone can remember. But when our conservation team scraped back the layers of paint last year, they discovered the ironwork had first been painted a deep green, and that's the shade you'll see there now. It's caused a few complaints, actually. Ruth: Then it's back up the hill to the Market Cross. You'll see people climbing the steps around the base hoping for a view, but to be honest, you can't see much from there; the buildings are too close. What makes the cross special is the bell at the top. The original was stolen in the nineteen seventies and never recovered. The one hanging there now was cast last year by a foundry in Devon, copied exactly from old photographs.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Round the corner from the cross are the Weavers' Cottages, a row of five little houses where cloth used to be made by hand. People are often disappointed to learn that they're all private homes now, so you can't just wander in. But the owners of the end cottage have very kindly agreed to let us in once a month, which means the only way to see inside is to book a place on one of our guided walks.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: And finally, there's the old Railway Goods Shed, down by the station car park. There's one of our audio posts inside, and if you press the button, you'll hear recordings we made with men and women who worked on the railway in the nineteen fifties and sixties.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: A lot of people ask me whether there's somewhere to eat in the shed. There isn't, I'm afraid, though the Signal Box Café is just over the road. And if you're after a view over the whole town, the best place is really the old water tower behind the station, but that's not part of the trail, because it isn't open to the public.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 17 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Ruth, tell us about those discs in the pavement.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Ah, the markers. Well, there was quite a debate about those. Some councillors wanted them made from recycled plastic, to be environmentally friendly, but in the end we went for bronze, because it lasts so much longer. They were designed by Ellen Marsh, a sculptor who's lived in Ashcombe all her life. They shouldn't need replacing for a very long time; we're hoping they'll still be there in fifty years.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: As for how long it takes, the leaflet says forty-five minutes, but that's if you walk briskly and don't stop at all. If you actually read the information boards, I'd allow about an hour and a half. Some people make a whole morning of it and have lunch at the end, but that's up to you.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: There's also a free app to go with the trail. Some people tell me they prefer it to the printed leaflet, but personally I find the map in the leaflet much easier to follow. There's a paid version of the app with extra content, too, but honestly, the free one has everything most visitors would need.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: My main piece of advice is this: the mobile signal in the old streets is terrible. So if you want to use the app, make sure you've got it on your phone before you leave home.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: And is there any way listeners can get involved?

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Well, we've had a wonderful response to our appeal for volunteer guides. In fact, we've got all the guides we need for this year, so thank you to everyone who came forward. Last year we asked people to suggest buildings to include, and that went well, too.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: What we're short of now is pictures. If you've got old photographs of the town in a drawer at home, shops, street parties, anything, we'd love to scan them for the trail website. You can drop them at the library, and we'll return them within a week.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Lovely. Ruth Penhale, thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Seminar Presentation: How Young Children Acquire Language
parts.context: Two students, Hannah and Liam, prepare a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Hannah and Liam, preparing a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 24.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay, Liam, we've got twenty minutes for the whole presentation, including questions, so we really need to decide what goes in and what comes out.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, fair enough. I made a list last night. Shall we go through it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Go on.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right, first, Chomsky, and the idea that we're born with some kind of built-in grammar.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Hmm. I mean, it's important, obviously, but everyone in the group did that to death in first year. If we spend five minutes on it, people will just switch off.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: True. So we cut it, then. We can mention his name in passing, but not give it a section. Next, kids who grow up with two languages.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I was wondering about dropping that, actually. It's such a huge area.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Ah, no, I really think we need it. Half the people in our seminar group grew up speaking more than one language at home. They'll want to hear about it.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Fair point. Keep it, but keep it short. What's next?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Children learning sign language. There's that brilliant study from Nicaragua.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd love to include that, but realistically, we'd have to explain how sign languages work first, and we just haven't got the time.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, you're right. It'd need a whole presentation of its own. And what about screen time, whether toddlers pick up words from the television?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd have said drop that, to be honest. The research is pretty thin.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: But that's kind of the point, isn't it? Everyone assumes educational programmes help, and the evidence says they mostly don't, not unless an adult is watching and talking about it with the child. That's a nice surprising finding. Just a minute or two. Hannah: All right, you win. And then babbling, which obviously stays. It's where everything starts.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Definitely.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay. Then the main section: child-directed speech. You know, the way adults talk to babies, with the high pitch and the exaggerated tune. Did anything in the reading surprise you?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: A couple of things. I'd always assumed it was mainly mothers who did it, and that dads sort of talked to babies the same way they talk to anyone else. But that study showed fathers change their voices just as much. That really surprised me.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Mm. What about the bit showing that newborns would rather listen to it than to normal adult speech? I thought that was amazing, at only a few days old.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Honestly, that didn't really surprise me. Babies like anything that sounds a bit musical. What did get me was that it isn't universal. I'd taken it for granted that every culture does it, but there are communities where adults hardly speak directly to babies at all, and the kids still learn to talk perfectly well.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Yes, that was striking. And older brothers and sisters doing it to toddlers, I found that quite unexpected.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Not me. I've got a four-year-old niece, and she talks to her baby brother exactly like that.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Fair enough. And the old claim that it holds back vocabulary?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Well, nobody really believes that any more. The studies show the opposite, which is pretty much what I'd have expected.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 25 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Now, about the video. I was planning to show that clip of my cousin's little boy, the one where he's naming everything in the garden.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It's lovely, but it's nearly ten minutes long, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Oh, I'd only play a minute of it, I can cut it down easily. And the sound's fine, I recorded it on a decent microphone. But I've decided not to use it after all. I mentioned it to my cousin, and she wasn't keen on her son being shown to a room full of strangers.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: No, absolutely, that's her call. We'll find something online instead.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Then I want to do the 'wug' experiment. You know, the one where kids are shown a drawing of a made-up creature called a wug, and then two of them, and they have to finish the sentence: 'There are two...'

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Isn't it a bit old, though? It was done in the nineteen fifties.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It's old, but it hasn't dated at all. I don't think there's anything that shows more clearly that kids aren't just copying what they hear. They've never heard the word 'wugs', so they must be applying a rule.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Some people say the results were overstated, though. That a lot of the kids were just guessing.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I've read that critique, and I don't buy it. The results have been repeated loads of times.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay. That leads nicely into mistakes like 'I goed' or 'two mouses'.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah. Parents get really worried about those.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And they correct them constantly, which, according to everything we read, makes almost no difference.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right. And people think they've stopped by about four, but actually some kids carry on making them till they're six or seven. Hannah: The point we need to get across is that they're not a sign that anything's wrong. It's the reverse, really: the child has worked out the rule and is just using it too widely. That's a step forward.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Agreed. That's our key message for that section.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: What about a handout? Last time the tutor said ours was far too long.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd rather not give anything out at the start. People just read it instead of listening.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: We could put all the references on the final slide...

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Nobody can copy down twenty references in the thirty seconds it's up.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Okay, so let's email a one-page summary to everyone once the session's over.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Yes, that's the best option.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'm a bit worried about questions at the end, though. What if someone asks something we can't answer?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: That doesn't bother me. We just say we'll look into it. And we've left five minutes, which is plenty. What I'm more concerned about is what happened last term, when we asked for questions and there was total silence. It was so awkward.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Oh, I remember. So should we get a friend to ask something?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Better than that, we'll finish with a question for them to discuss in pairs. That'll get them talking.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Right. So what next? Should we book a meeting with Dr Morgan to check the plan?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I don't think we need to. She said she's happy as long as we stick to the outline. And we can't really run through it properly till the slides are finished.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: True. The problem is, most of our sources are from the nineties. We need some recent research, especially on bilingualism.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Okay, let's both spend tomorrow in the library looking for studies from the last five years, and then meet up again on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Urban Heat Islands
parts.context: A lecturer in urban geography gives a talk on the causes and effects of urban heat islands and on ways of reducing them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a topic that's become increasingly urgent for city planners, and that's what's known as the urban heat island: the simple fact that cities are often a great deal hotter than the countryside around them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The difference can be dramatic. In extreme cases, a large city can be as much as twelve degrees warmer than the farmland that surrounds it. And here's what surprises most people. The gap isn't at its greatest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun is strongest. It's widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it has soaked up during the day for hours after sunset, while the countryside cools down quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what causes it? Well, the first factor is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces like asphalt and roofing tar absorb most of the sunlight that hits them, rather than bouncing it back. Scientists describe this property using the term albedo, that's A... L... B... E... D... O, which is simply a measure of how much light a surface reflects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Fresh snow, for example, has a very high albedo; it sends most of the light back into the sky. Asphalt, on the other hand, has an extremely low albedo, which is why a parking lot in July can burn your feet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second factor is the shape of the city. Tall buildings placed close together form what are called urban canyons. Heat bounces back and forth between the walls and gets trapped, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise carry that warm air away.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And third, there's what we call waste heat: the heat given off by human activity. You'd probably guess that traffic is the main source, and in a lot of cities, that's true. But in the case study I'll be referring to throughout today, which looked at a mid-sized city in Ontario, it wasn't vehicles that produced the most waste heat. It was industry, largely because of a cluster of factories right next to downtown. Air conditioning units came a fairly distant third.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the effects. The most obvious one is on health. Heat waves kill more people in North America each year than any other type of weather event, and the elderly are especially at risk, because the body's ability to cool itself declines with age.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But there's an economic side, too. When a city heats up, demand for electricity rises sharply, mainly because of all those air conditioners running at once, and utilities sometimes struggle to keep up. Natural gas use, by contrast, hardly changes at all in summer, so that isn't really where the costs come from.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also an effect on water that's often overlooked. When rain falls on hot pavement and rooftops, the water warms up before it drains into streams and rivers. And that's a real problem for fish that depend on cold water. In the Ontario study, researchers recorded a sharp decline in trout in the streams below the city. Not salmon, interestingly; they'd disappeared from that river long before the city expanded, so it's trout that are now under pressure.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, what can be done? Let's look at four approaches. The first is the cool roof. People tend to picture white roof tiles, but in fact most cool roofs are just ordinary roofs with a reflective coating applied on top, usually white or pale grey. It's cheap, it can go onto an existing building, and it can lower the surface temperature of a roof by thirty degrees or more.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second approach is the green roof, a roof planted with vegetation. Green roofs cool the air through evaporation, and they soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding. They're a lot more expensive than cool roofs, though, and many older buildings simply aren't strong enough to support the weight of wet soil.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third approach, and probably the one residents like best, is planting street trees. But not all trees are equally useful. The key thing isn't how tall a tree grows. What really matters is having wide canopies, that's the spreading layer of branches and leaves that actually throws shade onto the street. A tall, narrow tree like a poplar does surprisingly little.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the Ontario city, the tree-planting program was interesting because of where it was targeted. You might expect planners to start with the oldest neighbourhoods, or with the downtown core, where it's hottest. Instead, they focused on districts where people had a low income, because those areas had the fewest trees to begin with, and residents there were the least likely to own air conditioners.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The fourth approach is the cool pavement: road and sidewalk surfaces that are made lighter in colour. These do work, but they've turned out to have an unexpected drawback. On bright days, the light reflected off them creates glare, which pedestrians find really uncomfortable, and some studies suggest they can actually make people walking on them feel hotter, not cooler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So why haven't these measures been adopted everywhere? You'd assume the main obstacle is the initial cost, and that's certainly an issue. But the city officials interviewed in the Ontario study said that wasn't really what held them back. The bigger problem, they said, was maintenance. Reflective coatings get dirty and gradually lose their effect, and young trees need regular watering for several years. The money for that kind of upkeep just isn't there in most budgets.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay. Next week we'll look at how heat islands are measured, using satellite images and sensors mounted on buses. Please read chapter seven before then.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
